title: Basaltic Rocks Analyzed by the Spirit Rover in Gusev Crater
institution: Science / American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)

Authors: H. Y. McSween, R. E. Arvidson, J. F. Bell, D. Blaney, N. A. Cabrol, P. R. Christensen, B. C. Clark, J. A. Crisp, L. S. Crumpler, D. J. Des Marais, J. D. Farmer, R. Gellert, A. Ghosh, S. Published in Science, volume 305, issue 5685, pages 842-845 (2004), publisher American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3050842.

This record describes what the publication is about; the peer-reviewed full text is behind the DOI and was not ingested. Claims about the site's geology or history that cite this record should be read as 'this paper exists and studied the named site', not as a quotation of its findings unless an abstract appears below.

Abstract (from Crossref): The Spirit landing site in Gusev Crater on Mars contains dark, fine-grained, vesicular rocks interpreted as lavas. Pancam and MiniâThermal Emission Spectrometer (Mini-TES) spectra suggest that all of these rocks are similar but have variable coatings and dust mantles. Magnified images of brushed and abraded rock surfaces show alteration rinds and veins. Rock interiors contain â¤25% megacrysts. Chemical analyses of rocks by the Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer are consistent with picritic basalts, containing normative olivine, pyroxenes, plagioclase, and accessory FeTi oxides. MoÌssbauer, Pancam, and Mini-TES spectra confirm the presence of olivine, magnetite, and probably pyroxene. These basalts extend the known range of rock compositions composing the martian crust.
